questions.problem:
Find, in radians, the argument of $z=4+4\text{i}.$ 

**Hint**: The argument of a complex number is in the range $[0,2\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14226152/assets/fe0207214fb16ac0871e15f3be7c9fa33670a7df3617f5f9e0b92b45a09c76af.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $0<\operatorname{arg}⁡(z)<\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Further,

$$
\operatorname{arg}⁡(z)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{4})=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Argument of a Complex Number in the Second Quadrant
canonical_examples.problem: Find, in radians, the argument of $z=-1+\textrm{i}\sqrt{3}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14226152/assets/1bd35c5350e1dc1988cf98b8598a350701ef0b2a02a053b97ae2c89726de50c6.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\dfrac{\pi}{2}<        \arg(z)<        \pi.$ If $\alpha$ is the angle that $z$ makes with the negative real axis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\alpha  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1} \\ \alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta=\arg(z) = \pi - \dfrac\pi 3 = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14226152/assets/0095750158d9a296c9950c2d753ffe820735298c96cdf4de23aef0747862658d.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the third quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\pi<        \arg(z)<        \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.$ If $\alpha$ is the angle that $z$ makes with the negative real axis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta=\arg(z) = \pi +\dfrac\pi 6 = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find, in radians, the argument of $z=1-\textrm{i}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14226152/assets/5b9ec84d8c3176c85c1b5ea546fc138231a129a11b906d786578616a1dd16cb1.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant of the complex plane. Therefore $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}<       \arg(z)<       2\pi.$ 

If $\alpha$ is the angle that $z$ makes with the positive real axis, then

$$
\alpha = \arctan\left(1\right)  = \dfrac\pi 4.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta=\arg(z) = 2\pi - \dfrac\pi 4 =\dfrac{7\pi}{4}.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the complex number $z=3+4\textrm{i},$ as depicted on the Argand diagram below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14226152/assets/c857172451c97c24caab685a2f52097c0ca3c83df212c46a21f4a49c3edb19ca.png)

There is a natural angle $\theta$ that $z$ makes with the positive real axis. This angle is called the **argument** of $z.$ We often denote the argument as $\arg(z),$ or just $\theta.$ The numeric value of $\arg(z)$ is given in radians, and we restrict the values to 

$$
0\leq \arg(z) \lt 2\pi.
$$

In the triangle above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈0.93,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places. Therefore $\arg (z) \approx 0.93$ to two decimal places.

**Caution:** When you evaluate $\arctan \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ on your calculator, be sure that you're in radians mode, and be sure to put parentheses around the $\dfrac{4}{3}.$
